Jamaat-e-Islami’s *Rukniyyat*: Strength Within the Walls and a View Through the Window!!

Jamaat-e-Islami is an ideologically committed, cadre-based organisation. Within its organisational structure, *Rukn* (full member) represents the highest level of membership.

Rukns are generally regarded as key bearers of the organisation’s ideology, culture, and ethical standards. Consequently, they play a particularly important role in shaping the organisation’s public identity, image, and credibility.

Like every large organisation, Jamaat-e-Islami has ordinary members, workers, supporters, and well-wishers at various levels. Similarly, the presence of some unregulated supporters who actively promote the organisation on social media—often referred to colloquially as a “bot army”—cannot be denied. Of course, this phenomenon is not confined to Jamaat-e-Islami; to varying degrees, it can be observed among almost all political, social, and ideological organisations today.

The unrestrained remarks, emotionally driven behaviour, or online activities of some such supporters may place an organisation in an embarrassing position. Generally, however, their actions are not regarded as representative of the organisation’s official policies, positions, or organisational character.

The personal misconduct of a Rukn, by contrast, can naturally raise broader questions about the organisation’s ideological standards, the quality of its leadership, and the process through which its members are selected. For this reason, the selection of Rukns is not merely an organisational matter; it is also highly significant from ethical and strategic perspectives.

Based on my limited observations, it appears that, in a few exceptional cases, individuals have attained Rukn status without having developed the expected depth of commitment to the organisation’s ideology, principles, and methods of implementation.

Rather, an examination of their subsequent conduct, decisions, and organisational positions gives some grounds for the impression that, alongside ideological commitment, personal connections, social standing, influence, or other interest-related considerations may also have played a substantial role in their selection as Rukns.

Over time, the conduct of some such individuals has also suggested that, instead of prioritising personal development, self-purification, and meaningful contributions to the organisation’s ideological and institutional advancement, they have become relatively more focused on consolidating their personal positions, expanding their influence, or pursuing objectives connected with their own interests.

This creates a risk of adverse effects on the organisation’s ideological practice, internal culture, and long-term credibility.

It is important to clarify, however, that these observations by no means represent the overall picture of Rukns. They reflect an impression formed from a limited number of exceptional cases.

My personal observations have further led me to believe that such tendencies may be relatively more visible among some highly educated and professionally established individuals than among ordinary Rukns. This is not a conclusion based on statistical evidence, but an observation arising from limited experience that warrants verification through broader research.

In the cases of some such individuals, questions or controversies have also reportedly arisen at various times concerning their personal and family lives, professional conduct, financial dealings, or conflicts of interest. There have also been discussions about certain individuals having maintained relationships with different political or social circles in the past on the basis of convenience or personal advantage.

Nevertheless, given their higher education, status as ʿulamāʾ, social acceptability, or personal connections, there is room to question whether they have always been subjected to sufficiently thorough scrutiny.

Of course, it is neither particularly easy nor entirely realistic for a large organisation to investigate every aspect of every Rukn candidate’s life and activities with equal thoroughness.

In many cases, decisions have to be made on the basis of recommendations from responsible officials, personal familiarity, and the candidate’s own written self-reports. If such information is incomplete, exaggerated, or not fully consistent with reality, unsuitable individuals may gain access to important levels of the organisation. Accounts of such incidents have been heard from time to time.

There are also allegations in various circles that some individuals may not fully reflect reality when submitting personal reports or presenting information. Verifying the truth of such allegations is, of course, the responsibility of the organisation concerned.

If an individual views the organisation not as a means of implementing its ideology but as a vehicle for acquiring personal influence, status, or advantage, that person may gradually become a source of risk to the organisation as circumstances change.

The histories of various organisations show that, owing to a lack of ideological steadfastness or the predominance of personal interests, some members have subsequently changed their positions, creating difficult or embarrassing situations for their organisations. It would be difficult to claim that Jamaat-e-Islami is entirely immune to this general organisational reality.

At the same time, it must be acknowledged that it is virtually impossible for any large ideological, social, or political organisation to prevent the entry of unsuitable individuals with absolute certainty. Almost every major organisation in history has faced such challenges at one time or another.

Therefore, although eliminating this problem entirely may not be possible, the organisation’s long-term interests require an effective and institutionalised system that minimises opportunities for unsuitable individuals to gain entry and further strengthens its ethical, ideological, and organisational foundations.

In my view, relying solely on personal familiarity, educational qualifications, written self-assessments, or recommendations is not sufficient when selecting Rukns. In addition, there should be a mechanism for conducting, as far as possible, impartial, multidimensional, and evidence-based inquiries into a candidate’s personal character, ethical conduct, trustworthiness, financial transparency, professional integrity, and social standing. Such inquiries could draw on information from the candidate’s workplace, social circles, and other relevant settings.

Where appropriate, an effective system of periodic ethical and organisational evaluation of existing Rukns could also be considered.

Although this would not completely prevent unsuitable individuals from entering the organisation, it could substantially reduce the problem and further strengthen its moral standing, institutional credibility, and public trust.

These are simply a few observations and proposals offered by a well-wisher. My intention is not to disparage any individual or organisation, but rather to draw attention to the need to consolidate the long-term strength, credibility, and ethical standards of an organisation founded on ideological principles.
